claims.text: The kitchen does not publish a dedicated-fryer or cross-contamination policy, and the room is tiny with a shared cooking space, so celiac diners should confirm preparation directly before ordering.

Note that the soy hamburg steak plates and the burger-style mains are NOT on the restaurant's gluten-free list, and a reviewer reported that a hamburger here was not gluten-free — fried and breaded soy items in particular should be treated as containing gluten unless confirmed otherwise.

Soy-meat and stir-fried dishes are commonly seasoned with soy sauce, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. The restaurant does not document a wheat-free tamari substitution, so celiac diners should ask which seasonings are used on any soy-meat or savory plate.
The restaurant is 100% plant-based — every dish uses exclusively vegan ingredients — so there is no risk of cross-contact with animal products on the menu.

Staff speak English and the owner is fluent in Japanese, and the menu maintains a labeled gluten-free section, suggesting allergy questions can be discussed directly. The restaurant asks that allergen specifics be confirmed with them (zirael.q@gmail.com) since dishes contain soy products.
ZIRAEL explicitly offers a gluten-free menu and labels specific gluten-free items, including the ZIRAEL Plate, ginger-fried soy meat, ice cream, a vegan gluten-free canele, and most drinks.
The restaurant advertises dedicated vegan, vegetarian, gluten-free, oriental-vegetarian, and Muslim-friendly menus, indicating real experience accommodating dietary needs.
Being entirely plant-based makes it straightforward and reliable for vegan diners, with consistently warm reports about the welcoming owners.

Kura Sushi states its restaurants are not allergen-free or gluten-free environments, and that menu items may be prepared using shared equipment and fryers, allowing cross-contact with allergens including gluten. Even when an item is specially ordered, the company says it cannot guarantee it will be free of any allergen.

A conveyor-belt sushi setting means many shared surfaces and shared preparation areas, so celiac diners should treat the location as high cross-contact risk and confirm directly with staff before ordering.

Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Reports for Kura note that some locations may stock gluten-free soy sauce but availability is not guaranteed, so celiac diners are advised to bring their own. Sauced items such as unagi (eel) are coated in soy-sauce-based glazes that contain wheat.

Kura offers some plant-based and vegetable items, but the kitchen prepares fish, shellfish, egg, dairy and other animal products on shared equipment, so vegan diners cannot rely on the absence of animal cross-contact. Confirm specific items with staff.

An allergen menu and per-item allergen labeling are available to help diners identify which of the major allergens each dish contains, but staff and the company explicitly state they cannot guarantee any item is free of a given allergen.
The chain provides an allergen menu and labels the major allergens on its online menu, which makes it easier to screen dishes before ordering.

Dishes are made under the company's 'Muten' policy without MSG, artificial sweeteners, synthetic coloring or artificial preservatives - useful for diners avoiding those additives (note: this is separate from gluten/allergen safety).

This is a wheat-heavy kitchen, so it is not a safe choice for celiac diners. Several signature items are built on wheat gluten or wheat flour: the popular deep-fried kurumafu is a wheat-gluten product (one reviewer describes it as 'a little bit like seitan'), and the bakery (melon pan, cinnamon rolls) and the egg-salad sandwich on white bread are all wheat-based.

With wheat gluten (kurumafu/fu) and breads central to the menu, flour is present throughout the kitchen and airborne/surface cross-contamination is likely. Anyone with celiac disease should confirm directly with staff before ordering.

The menu includes curries, gimbap and other savory Japanese/Korean dishes that typically rely on soy sauce; most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. GF gluten content of the soy seasoning has not been documented, so celiac diners should confirm whether wheat-free tamari is used.
The restaurant is fully vegan, with an entirely plant-based menu and no animal products used on premises, so cross-contact with meat, dairy or egg is not a concern here.
Because the entire kitchen is vegan, plant-based diners can order freely across the menu without worrying about animal-product cross-contact.

This is a vegan cafe, not a dedicated gluten-free kitchen. Some items (such as rice bowls) are marked gluten-free, but wheat-based items like sandwiches, tartines, pancakes, muffins, cakes and tarts are made in the same kitchen, so cross-contact is possible. Celiac diners should confirm preparation directly with staff.
A gluten-free menu is listed among the cafe's options, but no detail on cross-contamination protocols is published.

No information on whether the soy sauce or seasonings used are wheat-free is published. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so celiac diners should ask whether tamari or a wheat-free alternative is used in any given dish.
The entire kitchen is plant-based: no fish, meat, eggs, or dairy are used anywhere on the menu, so there is no risk of animal-product cross-contact.
All dishes are described as fully vegan, with soy and oat milk alternatives used for drinks.
No specific allergy-handling protocols are published. English-speaking staff and an English menu are available, which can help when discussing allergies in person.
100% vegan kitchen, making this an easy and very low-risk choice for vegan diners.
Cooking focuses on naturally farmed organic vegetables and grains with no additives or artificial seasonings.
Some rice-based dishes are marked gluten-free, and a gluten-free menu is listed, giving GF diners a starting point to discuss with staff.
English-speaking staff and an English menu make it easier to confirm ingredients.
Not a dedicated gluten-free kitchen and not listed as a celiac-friendly place; staff understand 'wheat allergy' (the more common term in Japan) but do not cook in a separate GF environment.
Reviewers report the dosa is gluten-free and made separately from other items, but warn that the sambar served with it contains gluten.
Many curries are gluten-free, but diners are advised to check each one: some meat-based curries use the tandoor oven, which also cooks naan, so cross-contact is possible there.
Naan and other breads are wheat-based and should be avoided; a celiac reviewer was steered toward a tandoori set ordered without the naan.
Not every vegetarian dish can be made vegan; some curry bases contain ghee or other dairy that cannot simply be removed, so confirm dish by dish.

Staff speak English and the waiter was reported to understand cross-contact; the owner was described as very accommodating, explaining which curry set a gluten-free diner could safely order and what could and couldn't be eaten.

For vegans, staff are described as very helpful in explaining what can and cannot be made vegan, and confirmed details such as the pakora dips being vegan; most vegetarian dishes can be made vegan on request by specifying no dairy and no eggs. Vegan items are not labelled on the menu, so asking is necessary.
Many naturally gluten-free dishes (rice, dals, several curries) and an owner/staff who understand dietary needs and will guide GF diners toward a safe set.

Plenty of vegan-adaptable options including chana masala, aloo gobi, vegetable pakoras, masala dosa, tofu curry, and vegetable pilaf/biryani, with English-speaking staff who understand what vegan means.

VOG is a fully gluten-free-oriented kitchen that uses whole-grain and gluten-free flours, and gluten-free items are labeled on the menu. No source documents a specific cross-contamination protocol or a dedicated fryer, so celiacs should confirm prep separation directly with the owner, who is hands-on and explains dishes personally.

No source confirms whether any soy-based sauces used (for example in the 'butter soy meat' style curry) are wheat-free. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so a strict celiac should verify the specific sauce with staff.
The entire kitchen is vegetarian with no meat, fish or egg on the menu, which removes the usual animal cross-contact risks for vegans.
A reviewer advises ordering vegan choices through a person rather than the QR-code system to make sure specifications reach the kitchen.

The multilingual owner personally explains the dishes and is described as understanding vegan diets well, and reviewers call it super accommodating for gluten-free, vegetarian, vegan and Jain needs, with customizable spice levels.
100% vegetarian and vegan kitchen (no meat, fish or egg), so vegans avoid the typical animal cross-contact concerns.
Strong gluten-free orientation: gluten-free flours and labeled gluten-free items across the menu.
Hands-on, multilingual owner who explains dishes and accommodates vegan, gluten-free and Jain requests.

No reviews or sources describe the kitchen's cross-contamination practices, separate prep surfaces, or whether the savory menu is celiac-safe. The gluten-free claim is documented mainly for the desserts; for celiac diners, the safety of hot savory dishes cannot be confirmed from available sources.
Reviewers confirm the desserts are gluten-free, but none address whether they are prepared in a fully separate, dedicated gluten-free environment.

No source specifies whether the soy sauce or other seasonings used in savory dishes (such as the taco rice or curries) are wheat-free. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so celiac diners should confirm directly before ordering savory items.
The menu is reported to be clearly labeled, making it easy to see which items are vegan, and staff are said to understand what vegan cooking ("vegan ryori") means.
Daily blackboard specials follow a pattern where one option is always vegan-friendly.
Staff are repeatedly described as exceptionally friendly and accommodating, including preparing a vegan set that had sold out for one guest.

The cafe's sister dessert operation was built specifically around egg, dairy, and wheat allergies, indicating allergy awareness is central to the business, though no formal cross-contamination protocol is documented.
All desserts are 100% vegan and gluten-free, with nine such desserts available, and the dessert program was created expressly so people with egg, dairy, and wheat allergies can enjoy cake.
Vegan options are clearly marked and easy to identify on the menu, and staff understand vegan cooking.
The cafe emphasizes locally sourced ingredients and food that is gentle on body and mind, with vegan curry, taco rice, and pasta available.

This is a conveyor-belt (kaiten-zushi) restaurant, so plates of many different items pass continuously over your seat. That open belt creates real potential for cross-contact, so it is best treated as manageable for non-celiac gluten-avoiders rather than celiac-safe.

An allergen and ingredient chart is available in English on the Kura Sushi website; roughly a quarter of menu items are free of wheat, so a careful diner can build a meal, but should verify each item on the chart.

Kura makes its own soy sauce in-house as part of its no-additives policy, but this does not make it gluten-free, standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat. Assume the house soy sauce contains wheat and bring your own tamari or certified gluten-free soy sauce.

Some plant-forward plates exist (for example avocado-based rolls), but on a shared conveyor belt that carries fish and seafood, incidental cross-contact is likely; strict vegans should confirm preparation with staff.
Kura publishes a detailed allergen and ingredient chart in English on its website, which makes it easier than at most casual sushi spots to identify which items are free of wheat and other allergens.

The chain's founding principle is to avoid four common additives, MSG, artificial sweeteners, synthetic coloring, and artificial preservatives, drawing flavor from kombu and bonito instead, which appeals to diners watching what goes into their food.
